ety.text: From Middle English magen, mauen, mawe, mawen, mayen, maȝen, mouin, mow, mowen, moȝen, mugen, from Old English magan, from Proto-West Germanic *magan, from Proto-Germanic *maganą (“to be able, may”), from Proto-Indo-European *(me)mógʰe (“to be able”), from *megʰ- (“to be able”).
From French mai, so called because it blossoms in the month of May.

From Middle English may, maye (“woman, maid, girl, virgin”), from Old English mǣġ (“kinswoman”), from Proto-West Germanic *māg, from Proto-Germanic *mēgaz (“kinsman”). Related to Old English māge, mǣġe (“kinswoman”) and Old English mǣġ (“kinsman”).

senses.d: To be strong; to have power (over).
To be able; can.
ex: But many times[…]we give way to passions we may resist and will not.

senses.d: To be able to go.
ex:
O weary night, O long and tedious night,
 Abate thy houres, shine comforts from the East,
 That I may backe to Athens by day-light […].

senses.d: To have permission to, be allowed. Used in granting permission and in questions to make polite requests.
ex: you may smoke outside
may I sit there?

senses.d: Expressing a present possibility; possibly.
ex: he may be lying
Schrödinger's cat may or may not be in the box.

senses.d: Expressing a disjunctive or contrastive relation between indicative statements.
ex: You may be my boss, but that doesn't mean you can insult me.

senses.d: Expressing a wish (with present subjunctive effect).
ex: may you win;  may the weather be sunny;  long may your reign last
Let us pray that peace may soon return to our war-torn homeland.

senses.d: Used in modesty, courtesy, or concession, or to soften a question or remark.
ex: How old may Phillis be, you ask, / Whose Beauty thus all Hearts engages.

senses.d: The hawthorn bush or its blossoms.
ex: The fire from Lindfield was coming down the grassy hillside to the right between the hedges of may.

senses.d: To gather may, or flowers in general.
ex: In valleys green and still / Where lovers wander maying

senses.d: To celebrate May Day.
A maiden.

ety.text: From tal (“such”) + vez (“time”).
Inherited from Latin quid (“what”), but usurping all the roles of Latin quod. Cognate with English who.
From Old Galician-Portuguese que, from Latin quid (“what”) (usurping as well the roles of Latin quod), from Proto-Indo-European *kʷid, compare *kʷís. Cognate with English who.
Inherited from Old French aube espine, from Late Latin alba spīna, from Latin alba (“white”) + spīna (“thorn”). Cf. Italian albaspina, Catalan albespí.
Probably a calque of Medieval Latin albus spīnus (attested in the 11th c.), ultimately from Late Latin alba spīna. By surface analysis, bianco + spino.
From espina (“thorn”), on the model of Latin spīnus (“blackthorn, sloe tree”).

pt:estrepeiro.gl: may; hawthorn (shrub of the genus Crataegus)

phr: a cat may look at a king
gods may do what cattle may not

ety.text: Old French mairebor. Middle English maire English mayor From Middle English maire, from Old French maire (“head of a city or town government”), a substantivation of Old French maire (“greater”), from Latin maior (“bigger, greater, superior”), comparative of magnus (“big, great”). Doublet of major. Cognate with Old High German meior (“estate manager, steward, bailiff”) (modern German Meier), Middle Dutch meier (“administrator, steward, bailiff”) (modern Dutch meier).

senses.d: The chief executive of the municipal government of a city, borough, etc., formerly (historical) usually appointed as a caretaker by European royal courts but now usually appointed or elected locally.
ex: The office of mayor has been the tomb of many political ambitions.

senses.d: Synonym of mair, various former officials in the Kingdom of Scotland.
syn: various former officials in the Kingdom of Scotland

senses.d: A member of a city council.
A high justice, an important judge.
A largely ceremonial position in some municipal governments that presides over the city council while a contracted city manager holds actual executive power.
A local VIP, a muckamuck or big shot reckoned to lead some local group.
ex: In some parts the burlesque civic official was designated ‘Mayor of the Pig Market’.
The Mayor of Castro Street, that was Harvey's unofficial title.

From maire (“mayor”) + -esse (“-ess”).

ety.text: From Latin syndicus.

From alcalde (“mayor”) + -esa (“-ess”, feminine noun-forming suffix).

ety.text: Borrowed from Latin regentem.
From Old Galician-Portuguese prefeito, a borrowing from Latin praefectus (“overseer, director, prefect”).
From an ellipsis of Middle English it may be, equivalent to may + be. Compare mayhap.

senses.d: Perhaps, possibly.
ex: A small extra effort now can maybe save you much work later.
Maybe I was imagining it, but I could swear that the dog understood what I was saying.

senses.d: Perhaps that is true (expressing no commitment to a decision or a neutral viewpoint to a statement).
ex: Okay. See you later, maybe. — Maybe I’ll see you later.

senses.d: Certainly.
ex: Maybe not the best idea.

senses.d: Possible; uncertain.
ex: Then add those may-be years thou hast to live

senses.d: Something that is possibly true.
An answer that shows neither agreement nor disagreement.
ex: The results of the poll were inconclusive. We got two yeses, three nos, and four maybes.

senses.d: A future event that may or may not happen.
ex: About your raise: it's a big maybe.

ety.text: From peut (“(it) can”, “(it) may”) + être (“be”). Equivalent to Catalan potser, English maybe, Sicilian po siri ~ po (gghi)èssiri.

Borrowed from Greek μακάρι (makári, “I wish”), which is derived from Ancient Greek μακάριος (makários, “blessed, happy”). Compare Sicilian macari, Portuguese macar (“although”, conjunction), Spanish maguer (“although”, conjunction) and Romanian măcar (“even”, adverb).
From Vulgar Latin quī sapit (“who knows”). Cognate with Spanish and Galician quizá, Portuguese quiçá. By surface analysis, univerbation of chi + sa, literally “who knows”.
Inherited from Old Spanish quiçab, from qui sabe (“who knows”), ultimately from the Vulgar Latin expression qui sapit (“who knows”). Compare Italian chissà, Portuguese quiçá, and Catalan quissà.
Literally, “such time”.
From tal (“such”) + vez (“time”).
